title: Trust remains concentrated in competence-bearing professions and ordinary people while politicians, influencers, and AI chatbots face a credibility deficit
source_unit: Ipsos Global Trustworthiness Index 2026, 31-Country Global Advisor Survey
geography: 31 countries; 23,537 online adults under age 75 surveyed 19 June-3 July 2026

doctors.unit: percent finding doctors trustworthy on average across 31 countries

cross_country_convergence.value: doctors, scientists, and teachers are the three most trusted professions in all but four countries

observations.method: Ipsos global online survey asking respondents to rate professions on a five-point trustworthy-to-untrustworthy scale; global percentages are averages across 31 countries.
observations.uncertainty: Online samples, country weighting, translation, profession familiarity, and cultural interpretations of trust affect cross-country comparability; trust ratings are perceptions rather than verified competence or conduct.
observations.subgroup: Adults under 75 across 31 countries, with profession and country comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: High trust in doctors, scientists, and teachers may reflect role expectations and expertise, but it does not guarantee institutional satisfaction, policy agreement, or trust in every individual.

politicians.unit: percent finding politicians generally trustworthy on average

social_media_influencers.unit: percent finding social media influencers trustworthy

low_trust_pattern.value: politicians, influencers, and advertising executives are the three least trusted professions on average

observations.method: Ipsos five-point profession trustworthiness ratings aggregated across 31 countries.
observations.uncertainty: Low trust may reflect political conflict, role stereotypes, media exposure, or recent events; the index does not identify causes or distinguish different politicians, influencers, or advertising contexts.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 31 countries evaluating political, media, commercial, and social intermediaries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low aggregate trust can coexist with strong trust in particular local leaders, creators, or campaigns; broad distrust may also motivate scrutiny rather than disengagement.

observations.period: June-July 2026; AI chatbot and tech-entrepreneur trust

tech_entrepreneur_trust.value: 31% trustworthy versus 25% untrustworthy on average; ninth of 22 professions

us_tech_entrepreneur_gap.value: 22% trustworthy versus 38% untrustworthy in the United States

observations.method: New 2026 profession items added AI chatbots, tech entrepreneurs, and personal trainers to the Ipsos index; responses use the same five-point trustworthiness scale.
observations.uncertainty: AI familiarity, national technology culture, media narratives, and question novelty may affect results; trust ratings do not measure actual chatbot reliability or use.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 31 countries, with country contrast for the United States and regional patterns in AI skepticism.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low trust in chatbots may be a healthy demand for accountability and human oversight, but it may also limit useful adoption where AI can supplement scarce expertise.

observations.period: June-July 2026; ordinary-person and country trust geography

ordinary_person_trust.unit: percent saying the average man or woman in their country is trustworthy

ordinary_person_untrust.unit: percent saying the average man or woman is untrustworthy

country_index_leaders.value: India +20, Malaysia +16, Thailand +15, Singapore +12, Indonesia +9 on Ipsos net trustworthiness index

country_index_low.value: Poland and Romania -17; Argentina -12; Peru and Chile -13 on the Ipsos net trustworthiness index

observations.method: Ipsos country index subtracting untrustworthy scores from trustworthy scores across professions; ordinary-person results are reported separately from profession rankings.
observations.uncertainty: The country index is a constructed perception measure, not institutional performance or social-capital measurement; online coverage and country context limit direct causal interpretation.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 31 countries, including national and regional contrasts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Country-level profession distrust can coexist with interpersonal trust, as the LATAM results illustrate; institutional and everyday social trust should not be collapsed into one condition.

related_sources.claim: Ipsos What Worries the World provides complementary recurring public-concern and direction-of-travel evidence.
Edelman Trust Barometer provides complementary institutional, intergroup, and brand-trust evidence.
OECD trust survey provides complementary policy-performance and public-institution trust measures.

boundary: This record adds a profession, AI, intermediary, ordinary-person, and country-trust route. It uses Ipsos perception data, not verified competence, institutional performance, chatbot accuracy, interpersonal behavior, or causal explanation of regional trust differences.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ipsos Global Trustworthiness Index 2026 page and 13-page PDF were reviewed for field dates, sample, question scale, profession rankings, AI chatbot and tech entrepreneur items, ordinary-person trust, country index, and interpretation boundaries.
